_about: Human-curated parts of the Paradox Earth Discovery Cards. scripts/build_cards.py matches each entry to a region in site/data/regions.json by trend sign and centroid proximity (so this file survives a re-export that reorders region ids). Numbers are NEVER typed here: every number on a card is computed from site/data at build time. All literature (incl. the 'observations' cards) was checked against Crossref (DOI resolves, title/journal/year match) on 2026-11-15.

regions.title: The central Sahel got wetter, 2000-2025

user.who: An agricultural extension office in the central Sahel (e.g. a district extension team in Chad)
user.decision: Which millet and sorghum varieties and sowing windows to recommend to smallholders for the coming rainy season
user.why_it_matters: Advice built on the drought decades of the 1970s-80s may now be too conservative; a detectable wetting trend supports testing longer-cycle varieties, while year-to-year variability still argues for drought-hedged recommendations.

literature.citation: Biasutti, M. (2019). Rainfall trends in the African Sahel: Characteristics, processes, and causes. WIREs Climate Change, 10(4), e591.
literature.note: Reviews the partial recovery of Sahel rainfall since the 1980s drought, stronger in the central/eastern Sahel.

caveats: Percent changes look large in arid places because the baseline is small; read the mm/month figure alongside the percentage.
Sahel rainfall recovery is partial and uneven; the western Sahel has recovered less than the centre.
A wetter seasonal total can co-occur with more intense, less frequent storms; totals alone do not describe planting risk.

regions.title: North China and Mongolia got wetter, 2000-2025
regions.place: Northern and northeastern China and eastern Mongolia

user.who: A water-resources bureau in Inner Mongolia or northeast China (e.g. the Liao River basin)
user.decision: How to set seasonal reservoir operating rules and groundwater-pumping quotas, and how to size urban flood drainage
user.why_it_matters: A detectable wetting trend changes both sides of the ledger: more recharge opportunity, but also more flood-season water to route safely through cities.

literature.citation: Wu, K., Liu, H., Zhao, L., Lin, Y., & Yang, Z. (2022). The strengthening relationship between summer rainfall over North China and PDO since the mid-2000s. Frontiers in Earth Science, 10, 957940.
literature.note: Reports a significantly wetter period of North China summer rainfall since the mid-2000s, linked to the negative PDO phase (decadal variability, not necessarily a permanent trend).

caveats: The literature links this wetting to the Pacific Decadal Oscillation, so it may reverse when the PDO changes phase.

regions.title: The desert edge of the monsoon gets wetter
regions.place: Northwest India and Pakistan (Thar Desert and Indus plains)

user.who: A district disaster-management and irrigation planning office in Rajasthan or Sindh
user.decision: Whether to invest in flood drainage and rain-fed kharif crop advisories, rather than only drought relief, in a historically arid district
user.why_it_matters: Infrastructure in arid districts was designed for scarcity; a detectable wetting trend means more monsoon water arriving where drainage and crop calendars were not planned for it.

literature.citation: Joseph, L., Skliris, N., Dey, D., Marsh, R., Hirschi, J., et al. (2024). Increased Summer Monsoon Rainfall Over Northwest India Caused by Hadley Cell Expansion and Indian Ocean Warming. Geophysical Research Letters, 51, e2024GL108829.
literature.note: Satellite-era summer monsoon rainfall over northwest India and Pakistan increased markedly since 1979.

literature.citation: Jin, Q., & Wang, C. (2017). A revival of Indian summer monsoon rainfall since 2002. Nature Climate Change, 7, 587-594.
literature.note: Finds an Indian monsoon rainfall increase since 2002, focused on north-central India rather than this exact region.

literature.citation: Ullah, W., Karim, A., Ullah, S., et al. (2023). An increasing trend in daily monsoon precipitation extreme indices over Pakistan and its relationship with atmospheric circulations. Frontiers in Environmental Science, 11, 1228817.
literature.note: Increasing monsoon precipitation extremes over Pakistan; about extremes, not monthly totals.

caveats: Percent changes look large in arid places because the baseline is small; check the mm/month figure too.

regions.title: Northeastern Siberia gets wetter

user.who: A regional road and pipeline engineering authority in the Russian Far East
user.decision: Design-rainfall and culvert standards for infrastructure built on permafrost
user.why_it_matters: More summer water on thawing ground raises erosion and subsidence risk for roads and pipelines designed with older rainfall statistics.

literature.citation: Sun, C., Liu, Y., & Zhang, J. (2020). Roles of Sea Surface Temperature Warming and Loss of Arctic Sea Ice in the Enhanced Summer Wetting Trend Over Northeastern Siberia During Recent Decades. Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres, 125(18), e2020JD032557.
literature.note: Documents a summer wetting trend over northeastern Siberia (55-70N, 100-170E) over recent decades.

caveats: Rain-gauge coverage in northeastern Siberia is sparse, so the GPCP-based forcing leans on satellites and few stations.

regions.title: Central Siberia gets wetter

user.who: A river-shipping and hydropower operator on the Yenisei
user.decision: How to plan navigation-season dredging and reservoir flood-storage reserves
user.why_it_matters: A wetter catchment shifts the balance between low-water navigation risk and spring-summer flood risk.

literature.citation: Sun, C., Liu, Y., & Zhang, J. (2020). Roles of Sea Surface Temperature Warming and Loss of Arctic Sea Ice in the Enhanced Summer Wetting Trend Over Northeastern Siberia During Recent Decades. Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres, 125(18), e2020JD032557.
literature.note: Their wetting region (100-170E) lies east of this cluster; consistent in direction but not the same area.

caveats: Sparse gauges and snowfall undercatch make Arctic precipitation trends harder to verify.

regions.title: Western Sahel wetting rebound
regions.place: Western Sahel (southern Mali and Burkina Faso)

user.who: An agricultural extension office in southern Mali
user.decision: Sowing-date and variety advice for millet, sorghum and cotton farmers
user.why_it_matters: A wetting rebound can justify longer-season varieties, but only if it holds up under the checks below.

literature.citation: Biasutti, M. (2019). Rainfall trends in the African Sahel: Characteristics, processes, and causes. WIREs Climate Change, 10(4), e591.
literature.note: Recovery is documented across the Sahel but is weaker in the west than in the centre.

regions.title: Drying along the southern Andes
regions.place: South-central Chile to southern Patagonia (34-54°S, Chile and western Argentina)

user.who: A hydropower and water planner for the Biobío-to-Aysén river basins (Chile)
user.decision: How much water to allocate to irrigation and cities next season, and whether reservoir and desalination investments assume a drier baseline
user.why_it_matters: If the drying is a persistent trend rather than a run of bad years, water rights and reservoir rules that assume a return to 20th-century rainfall will over-allocate water.

literature.citation: Garreaud, R. D., Boisier, J. P., Rondanelli, R., Montecinos, A., Sepulveda, H. H., & Veloso-Aguila, D. (2020). The Central Chile Mega Drought (2010-2018): A climate dynamics perspective. International Journal of Climatology, 40(1), 421-439.
literature.note: Documents drying in central Chile (30-38°S); this cluster is mostly further south.

literature.citation: Garreaud, R. D., Alvarez-Garreton, C., Barichivich, J., et al. (2017). The 2010-2015 megadrought in central Chile: impacts on regional hydroclimate and vegetation. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 21, 6307-6327.
literature.note: Documents the megadrought core around 30-38S; this cluster extends further south into Patagonia.

caveats: Only part of this cluster lies in the 30-38°S core of the central-Chile megadrought studied in the literature; most of it is south-central Chile and Patagonia.
The literature attributes part of the drought to natural variability; Paradox Earth does not attribute causes.

regions.title: The southwestern Amazon is drying
regions.place: Southwestern Amazon (Rondônia and southern Amazonas, Brazil)

user.who: An agricultural climate-risk zoning analyst for Rondônia (Brazil's western soy, maize and cattle frontier)
user.decision: Which sowing windows and second-crop (safrinha) maize plantings to treat as high-risk in climate-risk zoning
user.why_it_matters: The second crop depends on rain at the end of the wet season; a detectable drying trend argues for shorter-cycle varieties or more conservative planting calendars.

literature.citation: Espinoza, J. C., Ronchail, J., Marengo, J. A., & Segura, H. (2019). Contrasting North-South changes in Amazon wet-day and dry-day frequency and related atmospheric features (1981-2017). Climate Dynamics, 52, 5413-5430.
literature.note: Dry-day frequency increased significantly over the southern Amazon, while the north got wetter.

literature.citation: Marengo, J. A., Jimenez, J. C., Espinoza, J. C., Cunha, A. P., & Aragao, L. E. O. (2022). Increased climate pressure on the agricultural frontier in the Eastern Amazonia-Cerrado transition zone. Scientific Reports, 12, 457.
literature.note: Strongest drying is in the eastern Amazonia-Cerrado transition, east of this cluster.

literature.citation: Marengo, J. A., Souza, C. M., Thonicke, K., et al. (2018). Changes in Climate and Land Use Over the Amazon Region: Current and Future Variability and Trends. Frontiers in Earth Science, 6, 228.
literature.note: Review: longer dry seasons in the southern Amazon; rainfall trends vary by dataset and region.

caveats: Land-use change and climate variability co-occur here; the trend is associated with, not attributed to, either.

regions.title: Drying along the middle Zambezi
regions.place: Middle Zambezi basin (southern Zambia and northern Zimbabwe)

user.who: A hydropower and water-allocation planner for Lake Kariba on the middle Zambezi (Zambia and Zimbabwe)
user.decision: How much reservoir drawdown to allow for electricity generation versus holding storage against dry years
user.why_it_matters: Zambia gets most of its electricity from hydropower; operating rules that assume past rainfall can empty reservoirs when a drying trend co-occurs with a dry year.

literature.citation: Hua, W., Zhou, L., Chen, H., Nicholson, S. E., Raghavendra, A., & Jiang, Y. (2016). Possible causes of the Central Equatorial African long-term drought. Environmental Research Letters, 11, 124002.
literature.note: Long-term drying over Central Equatorial Africa since the 1990s, mainly April-June and centred north of this cluster.

literature.citation: Zhou, L., Tian, Y., Myneni, R. B., et al. (2014). Widespread decline of Congo rainforest greenness in the past decade. Nature, 509, 86-90.
literature.note: Greenness decline consistent with decreasing rainfall over the Congo rainforest in 2000-2012; covers the forest core rather than the southern rim.

caveats: Rain-gauge density in south-central Africa is among the lowest on Earth, so GPCP-based trends here carry extra uncertainty.

retraction.title: Paradox Earth caught a false trend
retraction.headline_template: Paradox Earth caught a false trend: the apparent GLDAS-2.1 soil-water decline was withdrawn because it lines up with documented changes in the model's radiation forcing (level shifts around {breaks}) and disappears in a consistently forced NASA product (FLDAS, {fldas_window}: {fldas_slope} mm/decade, p = {fldas_p}, {fldas_verdict}).

user.who: Teachers and students using the Paradox Earth explorer
user.decision: Whether to trust a dramatic trend line before checking how the data were made
user.why_it_matters: A tool that rejects its own most exciting result shows why every trend needs a homogeneity check, not just a p-value.

literature.citation: NASA GES DISC. README Document for NASA GLDAS Version 2 Data Products (GLDAS-2.1 forcing section).
literature.note: States that the bias-correction scaling 'is unable to correct an apparent shift (of unknown origin) in the AGRMET climatology after 2011' for the radiation forcing.

literature.citation: Rodell, M., Houser, P. R., Jambor, U., et al. (2004). The Global Land Data Assimilation System. Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society, 85(3), 381-394.
literature.note: Describes GLDAS as a model driven by changing observation-based forcing, which is why its outputs need homogeneity checks before trend analysis.

literature.citation: Qin, T., Feng, J., Zhang, X., Li, C., Fan, J., Zhang, C., Dong, B., Wang, H., & Yan, D. (2023). Continued decline of global soil moisture content, with obvious soil stratification and regional difference. Science of the Total Environment, 864, 160982.
literature.note: Reports a GLDAS-Noah soil-moisture decline (0-200 cm, 2000-2020); our checks attribute the post-2010 part largely to forcing changes. Different question and method: they analyse the model record as given, we test it for forcing breaks first.

caveats: Withdrawn as a trend: the GLDAS-2.1 soil-water series is shown only as an example of a data artefact.
The 2011-2013 dip itself appears in both GLDAS versions, so it is likely a real dry spell; what is withdrawn is the long-term decline.
FLDAS and GLDAS share the Noah land model, so FLDAS is independent in forcing, not in model physics.
Precipitation (the variable we do report) comes from GPCP-based forcing and is checked for the same kind of break and against CHIRPS.

observations.title: GRACE sees what the soil model cannot
observations.place: Northwest India and eastern Pakistan (Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan; GRACE hotspot box 24-34°N, 68-80°E)
observations.headline_template: Over {years}, GRACE/GRACE-FO satellite gravity shows water storage over northwest India falling by about {grace_abs} mm per decade (mean of {n_boxes} 3-degree boxes, {n_sig} significant after false-discovery correction), while NASA's FLDAS land model, which has no groundwater pumping, shows soil water changing by {model} mm per decade. The missing water lines up with the groundwater depletion reported for this region in the literature.

user.who: A groundwater regulator or irrigation planner in Punjab-Haryana (e.g. a state groundwater authority)
user.decision: Whether to set or tighten groundwater extraction limits and crop-diversification incentives for over-exploited blocks
user.why_it_matters: Soil-moisture and rainfall products can look normal or even wet here while the aquifer is drawn down; an independent satellite measure of total water storage is the check that catches what those products cannot see.

literature.citation: Rodell, M., Velicogna, I., & Famiglietti, J. S. (2009). Satellite-based estimates of groundwater depletion in India. Nature, 460, 999-1002.
literature.note: GRACE-based groundwater depletion over Rajasthan, Punjab and Haryana (incl. Delhi), 2002-2008, attributed there to irrigation pumping.

literature.citation: Rodell, M., Famiglietti, J. S., Wiese, D. N., Reager, J. T., Beaudoing, H. K., Landerer, F. W., & Lo, M.-H. (2018). Emerging trends in global freshwater availability. Nature, 557, 651-659.
literature.note: Global GRACE trends 2002-2016; lists northern India among the largest water-storage declines, linked there to groundwater withdrawal.

caveats: GRACE mascons are a few hundred kilometres across; the box mean mixes irrigated plains with desert and foothills.
The northern boxes border the Himalaya; glacier mass loss can leak into them, so not all of the decline need be groundwater.
GRACE measures all water storage (groundwater, surface water, soil, snow and ice); this analysis does not separate them, and the cause is taken from the literature, not tested here.
Only one GRACE solution (JPL mascons) was analysed.
